newsitem.title: USA: Duke Power prepares for deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Duke Power prepares for deregulation.

text.p: Duke Power Co President and Chief Operating Officer Richard Priory said on Tuesday the utility expects to maintain its residential customer base once energy markets are deregulated by focusing on service.
He said Duke Power would not resort to gimmicks.

Deregulation has already thrown open the wholesale energy markets, enabling large operations such as factories to select an energy company from as far away as Canada. Now the residential customer is on the verge of doing the same.
"Our focus is to continue to be low cost provider in the Carolinas without using gimmicks," Priory said.
Duke Power's chief residential customer base is in North and South Carolina
"Customers can quickly see through gimmicks," Priory told reporters on a conference call from Duke Power offices here.
He said when the new market place gets defined Duke Power will bring all of its "innovative skills" to bear.

For example, the electric company's planned merger with natural gas company Panenergy Corp, announced late last year as a $7-billion stock swap, would allow the combined company to offer one-stop shopping to its customers.
"Duke and Panergy was put together with the idea that we would be able to create substantially more business than we could separately," he said.

Priory called the merger a "positioning move" to ensure that the merged company, Duke Energy, can thrive. "We have an interest in making sure that we have solid position in each of the energy markets around the country where we trade electricity and where we trade gas."
He said regulators and state legislators still have some quirks to resolve before the market can be successfully deregulated, citing reliability of power supply.
Priory also cited fairness and equity to all customers, particularly the poor and those in rural communities.

"If this thing is done properly, the concerns of that class of customer will be clearly addressed," he said. "A lot of people are worried because that class of customer is not at the table. That's exactly what we're talking about when we say we need comprehensive legislation."
